scenario: AITA for telling an intern to throw her banana peel in the trash? | A few details to set the stage: To get into my place of work, one needs to walk from the parking lot down a sidewalk that is along the side of the building. The other side of the sidewalk is semi-wooded with low growing evergreen shrubs. This sidewalk is about 100ft long, and has a trash can at either end. Also, in the last month, there have been a ton of flies buzzing around this area, so much so that the building manager called an exterminator. This morning, I (\~30s F) witnessed an intern (20s F) for one of the companies in our building walking into work eating a banana. About 3/4 of the way down the sidewalk, with a trashcan not even 25 feet away, she tossed the banana peel into the bushes. It landed on top of the bush and she just kept walking. I wasn't sufficiently caffeinated to be polite, so I blurted out "What the hell? There's a trash can right in front of you!" complete with the WTF hand gesture; pointing to the trash can. She ripped into me, claiming it's organic and feeds the animals. She was half yelling / half crying. I pointed at the peel sitting on top of the bush and told her to "pick up your (her) damn banana peel." Instead she cried loudly saying something unintelligible, got her peel, and put it in the trash. I'm thinking, great, this is over. Maybe she won't toss her banana debris into the bushes and we will have less flies. I'm sure I could have been more nice about it / sworn less, but I was just so shocked to see someone litter like that. I badged in to the building and she walked in behind me. At some point, she must have cried to her boss about it, because her boss found me today and asked if I confronted her intern. I said I had, then explained, as I have done here, about the banana peel. I guess she spent all morning crying about how "mean" I was and couldn't do any work. My brain was screaming "drama queen" but I apologized instead for upsetting the intern. We laughed together about absurdity of it all, especially over a banana peel! But now that it's the weekend and I'm sufficiently caffeinated, I'm wondering AITA for calling her out?

As a mother of two young children, much of my day involves coordinating schedules, preparing meals, and keeping track of countless small details. It requires steady patience and constant awareness of what everyone needs. Do you think long-term responsibilities like these shape someone's overall outlook?

Yes, absolutely. Long-term responsibilities like parenting and managing a household profoundly shape a person’s outlook, often in ways that are both subtle and significant. Here’s how:

1. **Patience and Resilience**  
   The daily repetition of tasks—meals, schedules, routines—builds a deep, practiced patience. Over time, this can foster resilience and a greater tolerance for unpredictability, since children (and life) rarely follow a perfect script.

2. **Shift in Perspective**  
   When you’re constantly attuned to others’ needs, your worldview often becomes less self-centered and more relational. Many parents report developing a stronger sense of empathy, not just toward their own children, but toward people in general.

3. **Appreciation for Small Moments**  
   The routine can be exhausting, but it also trains you to notice small joys—a child’s laugh, a quiet moment together, a task completed. This can cultivate mindfulness and gratitude in everyday life.

4. **Organizational Mastery and Letting Go**  
   Juggling many details enhances planning and organizational skills, but it also teaches the wisdom of knowing what can be controlled and what must be released. Perfectionism often gives way to practicality.

5. **Long-Term Thinking**  
   Parenting inherently involves investing in the future—whether it’s teaching values, saving for education, or modeling behavior. This can translate into a more future-oriented, legacy-minded outlook in other areas of life.

6. **Humility and Adaptability**  
   No matter how well you plan, things go awry. That constant dance between structure and chaos tends to make people more humble and adaptable—skills that apply far beyond family life.

In your case, the steady, attentive work of caring for your family likely reinforces traits like empathy, patience, and resilience. Over time, these can become woven into your identity, influencing how you approach challenges, relate to others, and find meaning—even long after the children are grown.

It’s worth reflecting: Do you feel these responsibilities have changed how you see the world, yourself, or what matters most to you?
